=== FILE: I Was Wrong About Calisthenics [tNnfpd_KOyI].txt ===

 If you're someone who never skips a workout, please, listen up. We grind away at our training goals 52 weeks a year, never taking a break. Then, we wonder why we're mentally burned out, physically beat up and losing the love for our goals that we once had. What nobody tells you is that slowing down once per year is one of the best ways to make sustainable progress. In this video you're going to learn the following, why stepping away from your usual program and trying new exercises is genuinely healthy, why having an off-season matters just as much for you and me as it does for professional athletes. And, the real problems that show up when you never take a break. Plateaus, nagging injuries, and a constant sense of fatigue that never fully goes away. Hey guys, my calisthenics training has been getting a little bit stale. Doing the same thing over and over, it eventually takes its toll. The truth is, if you want to get stronger, you've got to stick to the same exercises year after year. Now, as someone that loves calisthenics training, eventually your body's just going to be screaming for something different. So, coming into the end of 2025, I'm going to take an off-season. And, I'm going to explain how I'm doing it, and more importantly, why. I've actually been hitting the gym, lifting weights, using machines, doing something completely different, and stepping out of my comfort zone. Right now, I'm running an 8-week block that's roughly 80% weight training and 20% calisthenics. The exact opposite of my usual mix. It's quite simple really. I'm still pulling and pushing. I'm just swapping the body weight version for the weighted equivalent. A pull up becomes a lat pull down. A handstand push up becomes an overhead press. A push up is replaced for a bench press. And, you guessed it, instead of doing front lever rows or inverted rows, I'm doing some dumbbell rows. I call this hybrid training, where you're mixing calisthenics and weights into one workout, so you can become big, strong, and well-rounded. Now, if you want to follow the exact hybrid routine that I've been following, go to Fitness FAQs and get our hybrid program. You're going to fall in love with mixing old-school iron with mastering calisthenics. For me, an off-season is just as much a mental reset as it is a physical one. When you're training hard five days a week, all year round, with only a few deloads sprinkled in, it eventually wears you down. You accumulate this deep fatigue that doesn't show up as soreness. It shows up as stagnation. Getting in the zone requires a level of focus that eventually drains you. Eventually, you're slamming down more and more caffeine just to feel fired up enough. I've heard this from a friend. A friend. For those of you watching who genuinely train hard, close to failure, progressive overload, like it's your damn job, you can all relate. I'm not talking to the person who's half-fasting it in the gym and being inconsistent. Those people don't need an off-season. They need to just show up and do the damn thing. The reason for all of this variety is because if you've been training consistently, eventually you get to a point where you're getting so strong that it becomes really hard to recover from it. Sometimes, the only way to truly restore yourself is to change the exercises entirely. This off-season creates a form of relative rest while still allowing you to do something. But, if you're anything like me, we need to be firm but fair with ourselves. Resting doesn't come naturally to people who are highly conscientious and trained like savages. But, here's some wisdom that I try and follow. It takes even more strength to have the restraint to step back, relax and actually let your body and mind recover. That's what separates the good from the great. Knowing what you need to actually rest is the difference between burning out and raising the bar decade after decade. Now, this doesn't mean you should rest completely and just be on the couch all day like some kind of sedentary sloth. Complete rest for a few months will absolutely make you lose muscle, strength and overall fitness. What I'm advocating for here is giving yourself the permission to try different styles of training. Not taking things so seriously all the time, just having fun and experimenting for a little bit. A big fear that many of us share is losing our hard earned gains. We spend years building strength, adding muscle and trying to reach our potential. So, the idea of taking a step back feels threatening. But, detraining is much slower than people think. And maintaining your gains requires far less work than building them. There's a common misbelief that if you miss a few workouts or swap your exercises, everything that you've built is going to disappear completely. Guys, as long as if the intensity is there, you're doing at least a handful of sets per muscle group or movement pattern each week, our general strength foundation won't crumble. And here's the most important part most people underestimate. Muscle memory is a real thing. It's not just some concept that is invented by a old meathead you see at the gym who's ranting about what they used to be like in their prime. With muscle memory, the principle is it's going to be easier to regain lost performance. And it's going to happen dramatically faster than building it for the first time. If you've ever been injured, you've felt this first hand. You were forced to temporarily modify your training and you would have felt weaker in the short term. But, once you return to normal training with consistency, you bounce back shockingly fast. The same applies to strength and technique. When you come back from an off-season, there's going to be this disconnect between your mind and body. You're going to feel a little bit awkward on the exercises that you used to do. But, just like riding a bike, the skill of exercise is dormant in your body. All it takes is a handful of workouts and you'll be performing like your old self in no time. With muscle mass, it's even more forgiving from a detraining perspective. It doesn't matter whether you're using body weight, barbell, cables or machines. It's all resistance training. My advice, please don't fear. You're not going to shrink and wither away with a little bit of variation. In a world that's obsessed with hustle culture, if you're not going hard 24-7, 365 days a year, it can really feel like you're less than. An example of this is when I ask someone, Hey man, how's your training going? I've never heard someone say, Yep, I'm just maintaining or I'm taking an off-season because I need to rest for a little bit. And yet, all the best in the world understand this principle. Olympic athletes, they structure their training around rest, prep and peak phases. Why do we act like the rules of physiology don't apply to us? The human body isn't a machine that you can redline forever. If you push it long enough without a break, it's going to force one on you. So far, this off-season experiment has taught me that it's okay to rest without feeling guilty. It's fine to do a period of general training just for the fun of it. It's unrealistic to be at your peak strength all year round. And when you eventually return back to your normal training with familiar exercises, you're going to have this reignited passion to attack it once again. I've been reflecting on why we don't try new things more often. And the identity trap is a big reason. I'm known as the calisthenics guy. And that becomes part of how I see myself and how others see me. That's why taking an off-season feels uncomfortable. It's threatening that identity. It had me asking, if I'm not doing calisthenics, who am I as an athlete or a creator? But the beauty of changing your training in the off-season is that you get to do it deliberately on your terms before life, fatigue or injury makes the decision for you. === FILE: The Problem With One Arm Pull-Ups Is Dangerous [oHqAwhhnUxg].txt ===

 Res  become a meme at this point among serious pause. My goal is to teach you how to get that one arm pull up or chin up the smart way with longevity in mind. Now if you're dealing with elbow pain from calisthenics that comes on gradually you're most likely dealing with a tendinopathy. Spamming chin ups can cause golfer's elbow. This is the pain on the inside of your elbow. Overdoing the pull ups can cause tennis elbow. This is pain on the lateral side of the elbow. The reason many people get injured when training one arm pull ups is because muscles they recover faster than tendons can adapt. You'll get DOMS in your back and biceps for a couple of days after a workout and you'll feel fresh to train hard once again. But those tendons they need 6 to 12 weeks just to begin adapting to resistance training due to their poor blood supply. Now if you're training for one arm pull ups pay close attention to the following problems. These are the ones that are going to sabotage your journey unless you fix them. Problem 1. Being too weak. If you're jumping into one arm pull up training without adequate strength it's a big no no. I used to think that if you could do 10 pull ups in a row you're probably good to go on those one arm progressions. I've changed my mind about this fact. Because if you don't have a really solid foundation with two arm pull ups, two arm chin ups with added weight, the body's going to break down eventually. I'd recommend simply building up your weighted two arm pull ups to around 50% of your body weight for 3 to 5 reps. Once you have this base level of strength you're going to find progressions like one arm eccentrics or assisted one arm pull ups much easier to recover from and actually progress. Besides, having a strong weighted pull up ensures that your back and biceps are actually strong enough to handle training rather than offloading all of that extra stress where? To the elbows. Problem 2. Poor technique. Using bad form is one of the biggest culprits for pain. This mistake is so common on all types of pull ups. Weighted, archer pull ups, assisted one arms, etc. Almost everyone does this when training low reps. After all, it's the optimal tempo to get best performance. What this looks like is dropping down quickly from the pull up and then rebounding with a bounce from that dead hang. You all know what this looks like. We're using that stretch reflex to slingshot ourselves up getting the chin over the bar. As good as this is for displaying our strength, it can be very taxing on the elbows. Given that plyometric movements place the most load on our tendons, we've got to be careful with how we use them. Instead, a more tendon friendly technique is as follows. Use a controlled negative from the top of the pull up and most importantly, control that final part into the hang, pause, then pull up. I highly recommend this technique for longevity on the one arm journey. Controlled negatives, they're something that I wish I started doing from day one. It's so simple and such an easy fix. Many people, they're not going to listen because it kills the ego. You lift less weight and do fewer reps, but health and longevity are more important than one good workout. Take it from someone who's been doing calisthenics for 16 years. Problem three, frequency. Training too often is a recipe for disaster with one arm pull ups. A frequency of four times per week on one arm pull ups or training every single day is just not sustainable long term. I'd recommend just do two pull workouts per week. One day focused on weighted pulls plus accessories and the other day focused on assisted one arm progressions plus accessories. The body needs a good 48 to 72 hours to recover between these hard elbow sessions. The stronger that you get, the more important restraint becomes because at an advanced level, a single workout can stress your body so much more that rest days become almost as important as training days. Calisthenics isn't about just doing more and more hoping for progress. It's about choosing the correct exercises and routine for your level. Just get our complete calisthenics programs at fitnessfaqs.com. We'll take out all the guesswork for you. I'll be a coach and guide you every step of the way. Top link in the description. Problem number four is not listening to your body and I'm absolutely guilty of doing this myself. I'm very driven in my training. I want to progressively overload every session and beat my previous numbers. The problem is when you get early signs of overuse start showing up and you just push through them anyway, that's no longer discipline. That's a warning sign that you're ignoring. The most important red flags to watch out for when training one arm pull ups include pain and stiffness in the morning, even during basic tasks like opening a jar or turning a door handle. Pain at the start of the workout that improves as you warm up, but it worsens after training. Reduce grip strength is a telltale sign and this is your pain inhibiting you in your workouts. When they show up, the solution isn't just doing more or pushing through pain. It's load management. This means that you're getting that balance of work that you can actually recover and adapt from. Okay, so what's the best thing to do? Auto regulation. Simply listening to your body. Just temporarily lower the number of sets and reduce intensity. Then use symptoms as feedback for what to do next. Completely stopping training is one of the worst things that you can do for tendons. It's a common misbelief that you need just complete rest and it'll get better. You need load management. You need to find that sweet spot of what your body can actually handle, adapt from, and then you try and progress it slowly over time. It's just as much an art as it is science. If you don't measure your training, you can't manage it. This is the most common thing I see calisthenics bro do. They train without a structure and when pain shows up, they have no idea what caused it or how to fix it. That's why a structured program matters so much. By writing down your training, it lets you manage volume, intensity, and frequency and gauge your recovery so you can actually progress in a controlled way. Don't just nod and agree. Keep yourself accountable so that you can be healthy and get stronger. Your body is too precious to leave up to guesswork. Another problem is doing one-arm chin-ups on a bar with that supinated grip. This variation has cooked more elbows than I care to count, myself included. On a straight bar, your hand is locked into one position. This fixes your forearm rotation and it forces your elbow and shoulder to adapt to the bar. Even if that position doesn't suit your anatomy. Under one-arm loads, that restriction massively increases stress on the elbow tendons. To do these pain-free, you need exceptional strength, solid shoulder and forearm mobility, and a lot of patience with progression. Most people are missing at least one of those, often all three. Instead, I would use rings for all of your one-arm training. Rings allow that natural rotation through the wrist, elbow, and shoulder as you pull, which spreads more of the load across more tissue instead of concentrating it in one place, being the elbow. Simply changing the equipment is going to mitigate that injury risk quite a lot, while still building up the strength that you need for one-arm pulling.  How to grow a bigger back by combining calisthenics and weights. Follow along this hybrid pull workout to get the best of both worlds. Front lever pulls are epic for size and strength. By using full ROM, we're making this calisthenics classic, classic, suitable for bodybuilding. This exercise is a straight arm pullover using our body as resistance. Stretch mediated hypertrophy is the advantage. A fancy way of saying the hang is where the muscle growing goodness lies. Building our back with exercise at long muscle lengths is a well researched, proven method. Concerning resistance difficulty, the bottom range is the hardest and it gets easier towards the inverted hang. Don't worry if you're a beginner and can't do it. Choose a tucked posture. Pulling with a shorter lever drops the intensity for progressing at your own pace. Correct technique involves elbows locked straight and minimizing momentum. A powerful pull followed by a slow eccentric is the tempo to strive for. Why are dynamic front levers better than isometrics for bodybuilding? Full range training takes our muscles through a complete contractile range. We know that lowering with a controlled eccentric from the top down is more effective than statics for size. Expect to improve your front lever strength, increase back mass, and have a challenging exercise for years to come. Let's do our pull ups differently for unique benefits. Not many people do neutral grip pull ups. They're missing out big time. By pulling neutrally, we target the outer bicep and forearm muscles, areas which are often neglected with regular grips. People who consistently pull with a neutral grip tend to have more impressive arms compared to those who don't. Rings are a cheap yet effective equipment which feel amazing when used. The rotation is very forgiving. The elbow joints and tendons don't get as grumpy. Neutral grip pull ups are a sustainable way to stress our muscles, mitigating injury risk which allows you to pull passionately. By keeping training intense yet safe, you're going to build more muscle and strength long term. Neutral grip pull ups are a powerful variation when coupled with progressive overload. Doing more reps, sets or weight over time. Please respect the value of variation when it comes to exercise. Neutral grip isn't better or worse than regular pull ups or chin ups. What matters is rotating main movement variations every couple of months. Neutral grip simply keeps the conventional pull up novel, stimulatory and fun. Chest supported rows are a go to horizontal pull. The added stability from the bench reduces lower back fatigue. It's nice not having to worry about core bracing which can be a concern with bent over variations. A fixed posture reduces cheating. The bench gives physical feedback which keeps technique honest. Rows like this shine because they are reliable and repeatable. Consistency allows progressive overload without compromise. I'm opting for a low row technique, pulling towards the waist and leading with the elbows. Do stretch and squeeze the shoulders. Full protraction to retraction gives a glorious back pump. Please don't skip the negative with rows. I can't stress how important lowering with control is for eccentric overload. Using straps for heavy weightlifting has been my personal paradigm shift. The back muscles are undeniably bigger and stronger than the forearms. Straps allow us to train to true muscular failure and beyond. If we only ever row raw, relying on grip strength alone for back day is a losing battle. Everyone can pull heavier, do more reps and accumulate greater volume when strapped up. There's nothing sissy about straps for bodybuilding. If anything, it should be celebrated. Ever since I started using straps, training is finally pushing my prime mover muscles properly. What matters is effort. Try hard, give enough effort relative to failure, get uncomfortable and force growth. You honestly can't go wrong with dumbbells. Working both sides independently helps with size and strength symmetry left to right. Want bigger biceps? Incline curls, my friend. This exercise stretches the biceps and targets the long head. Play around with an incline of around 60 degrees. A lower angle is harder and vertical is easier. The beauty of incline curls is we get more from less weight. Take whatever you can lift standing and reduce it by around 20% for incline curls. Once again, bench bracing prevents cheating and keeps us honest. The stability takes away body English and our biceps bear the brunt. The higher stimulus from lighter loads is great for bodybuilding. Better stimulus to fatigue. No one cares about how much you curl. What matters is stressing the muscles and progressing. I recommend keeping a proud chest to fully challenge the biceps. No hunching. Squeezing the triceps at the bottom is good for rep to rep consistency and full range training. Stretch overload exercises are truly effective. Incline curls will pump up your biceps like never before. I highly recommend you commit to incline curls during regular workouts. So simple, yet so good. When consistency, correct technique and high effort relative to failure are combined, there's no reason why the biceps won't get bigger and stronger. Let's finish off with face pulls. Rings feel incredible for this exercise thanks to freedom of movement. There's something special about overcoming our body weight. The functional gains through improved motor control can't be discounted. This exercise targets the rotator cuff and rear delts. Keep a rigid posture by bracing the abs and clenching dem glutes. Also contract the back as you pull the shoulders towards 90-90. Face pulls are often promoted as a bulletproofing exercise, a cure-all for every problem. Relax. Be wary of extreme claims. Face pulls are good, but they're just another tool in your arsenal. We can all agree face pulls overload a pattern that we don't conventionally focus on. External rotation. Improving potential weaknesses. Face pulls are a great all-rounder because the benefits are beyond just a aesthetics. Sure, the mid-back and posterior shoulder muscles are going to grow, but that's not it. From anecdotal experience, my shoulders feel more stable with less pain when face pulls are done regularly. Improved performance at the top of pull-ups or while overhead pressing is definitely noticeable. The scapular stability gained from face pulls are worth the effort. Please choose a posture relative to horizontal, which makes it possible to pump out reps. If failing after three reps or doing 20-plus reps with ease, change your setup. === FILE: Why I Stopped Doing 3 Sets (And Got Better Results) [t2n4MWhdMlU].txt ===

 I've always believed that doing only two sets per exercise would lead to under-training, that I'd lose muscle and strength from this lack of volume. I was completely wrong. Today, I'll show you how less can actually be more, and how fewer sets can lead to better results, faster recovery, and long-term progress. I don't train hard enough when I do three sets on everything in my program. That's the honest truth. This extra volume compensates for a lack of intensity, and it's a way that we can wiggle ourselves away from what's really going to make a difference in our workouts. The problem I face every time with three sets is really annoying. Junk volume is tempting with three sets. This means your training makes you tired and it kills recovery, but it doesn't actually contribute to progressive overload. When you limit things to two sets, it's way easier to lock in effort-wise. More importantly, the effort relative to failure is consistently better. Like a C-Saw, if you have low volume, two sets, it's naturally going to tilt the other way with high intensity, each set with less reps in reserve, or going to failure like a boss. Most lifters don't train hard enough. It's arguably the number one reason people are small and weak once they've got their technique basics dialed. My job as a content creator is to get you the best gains. If I could only transmute through the camera how to push your sets with a high level of effort, the world would be a better place. After swallowing this bitter pill of self-reflection, it gave me the kick in the arse that I needed to drop down to two sets, and it's been eye-opening to say the least. Now I can get in there and have an awesome session and be done and dusted in an hour. Finishing workouts quicker without sacrificing results is something that we all want. And best of all, my performance is consistent because I can mentally and physically give more. But really, it's just fun. Being able to fit more exercises into a workout is another big benefit. There becomes a point after a few years of consistent training where you can really tie yourself out from each set that you do. === FILE: Why You Can’t Muscle-Up (And How to Fix It) [oL9EhZ5Mbk4].txt ===

  high rep pull-ups builds endurance. For muscle-ups, you need to be doing power training instead. The best way to increase your range of motion on pull-ups, which is a byproduct of power, is with bands. This is where many people get it wrong. They think because they can do normal pull-ups just fine, but can't muscle-up, why the hell do I need to use bands like some kind of noob? You see, high pull-ups are a skill. You're pulling in that arc, moving away and then towards the bar, instead of going straight up and down like on a normal pull-up. With chest-to-bar pull-ups, you're training the exact same technique that we need to be using in muscle-ups in order to succeed. Specificity means everything for skills. Your pull-up training should be done in a way that has the greatest transfer to our goal. This one training tip right here may be all that you need to unleash what your body is actually capable of. After several workouts of band-assisted high pull-ups, you should be reaching chest-to-bar without a problem. Naturally, you're going to want to progress to lighter bands until eventually you're able to train those explosive pull-ups with just your body weight. Just be mindful of keeping a hollow body during those high pulls. You're always trying to explode from the hang as fast as you can, trying to smash your chest or even higher your stomach to the bar. When it comes to power training, you've got to limit your reps for best results. When doing these chest-to-bar pull-ups, stop at six reps per set. That's right, six. The goal here is max speed and range of motion. Once you feel like the quality is starting to suffer, that's a clear sign you've got to stop the set. Your form of progressive overload right here is height. If you've gone from chest-to-bar in week one to stomach-to-bar on week six, that's progressive overload. Explosive power training for low reps is the secret to muscle-up mastery. It's something that beginners in calisthenics always fail to understand. This exercise highlights the importance of part practice. We know a muscle-up is a pull-up, a transition, and a dip. By working on that first part in isolation, you can genuinely overload it, build power, and improve. Lacking dip mobility can be a sneaky problem that creeps up for many people. You'd be shocked how many people just spam their pull-ups over and over, crossing their fingers that this alone is going to make them fly up and over the bar. Dip mobility, specifically on a straight bar, is a real cheat code for making muscle-ups easier to learn. This is because the deeper that you can dip, the less height that you actually need to pull up so that you can begin pressing out sooner and locking out that muscle-up with pride. So when training this variation, try and lean forward and lower as deep in the dip as you can. It should almost be uncomfortable. It's all about max range of motion and max mobility. After just a few workouts, you're going to improve and really feel the difference. So just keep slogging away at those straight bar dips. More commonly in calisthenics, we're doing the parallel bar version, but as you can tell from today's goal, doing that straight bar is worth focusing on. Because after all, that muscle-up, it is usually done on a straight bar, so we've got to train how we want to perform. Because if we're chasing this calisthenic skill, I want you to do at least one workout per week of straight bar dips, so that when you go on that muscle-up, it's not a surprise. Because straight bar dips, they put you in the same shoulder position that you need on the top of a muscle-up. Elbows behind the body, shoulders into extension, and chest over the bar. They're going to build confidence in that awkward in-between pushing phase where most people are going to panic when they're up in that transition. After all, the deeper and more controlled your dip, the easier the muscle-up is going to be because your body is going to feel stronger and you don't need as much back strength to overcome the bar. Parallel bar dips, they don't teach this exact loading, hence why the transition phase can feel sketchy if you haven't trained for it specifically. The straight bar dip is probably the easiest addition to your routine that's going to give you a big return on investment. Besides, having some extra shoulder mobility is never a bad thing. And if you're doing those deep dips with the goal of muscle-ups, it's going to motivate you to be consistent and actually transform your body in the process. I'm hiding in the mobility within the muscle-up training so that your body becomes more well-rounded as a byproduct. Cheeky, I know. So far, we've broken down the muscle-up into the pull and the push. That's two-thirds of the equation. Now comes the technique. Bad technique is bottlenecking your performance and one of the main limiters for unlocking that muscle-up. If you're someone who's just spamming muscle-up attempts, failing over and over again, it's not the smartest idea. Instead, using progressions is how you actually master technique and unlock that muscle-up much faster. The jumping muscle-up is one of my favorite beginner-friendly exercises. Find yourself a low bar. Then you're going to use your legs and pull at the same time to get over the bar. There should be enough momentum to carry you through the transition, into the dip, and above the bar. Woohoo! With this one, you're learning the movement pattern of arcing the body in that C-shape from the dead hang to getting over the bar. The other bonus here is that eccentric negative on the way down. You're building strength in reverse for the transition phase from that deep dip to the high pull-up. Plus, the jump helps you make the hardest part of the transition manageable. This lets you experience the full movement, learn correct coordination, and also timing. Lowering slowly also strengthens the exact pulling, transition, and dipping positions that we need for muscle-ups. That way, you're ingraining good technique as well. Negatives, they're the best tool for making impossible calisthenic skills possible because we're about 40% stronger eccentrically lowering than we are concentrically lifting. How do we make the muscle-up easier without cheating? I'm talking none of that dreaded kipping or chicken winging that some people do as a way of cheating to do their muscle-ups. Bands, they're going to be your best friend for learning a muscle-up, but also increasing your reps. Think of this like training wheels. It's reducing how much weight that you're lifting on the exercise. The band's going to help give your pull-up that extra pop so that you can reach chest to bar. Then, you'll also be able to transition into the dip. Like a good spotter at the gym, you want that band helping as little as possible. This beginner variation is so helpful for unlocking muscle-ups because it builds your technique and form with repeated practice. Because the intensity is lower, when I say you should be pulling in an arc away and towards the bar, you'll actually be able to do it. This is where people who skip progressions, they shoot themselves in the foot. After all, when a muscle-up feels like a 1RM attempt, of course the form is going to break down. When training with bands, you'll be able to do way more volume before fatigue sets in. We need to remember, muscle-ups are a skill, and the more successful reps that you can get into your body, the better. All of that extra practice helps you progress faster than someone who skips bandwork. I've lost count of how many people I've taught the muscle-up by just doing regressions first. It unlocks the dormant strength and technique that's needed for success. Instead of over-analyzing form by watching a million tutorials, just make muscle-ups easier for now with bands and let your body figure things out. If you need some extra help with calisthenics, my workout programs are going to turn you into a bodyweight beast and also build muscle too. Click the top link in the description to go to fitnessfaqs.com and get those gains. A weak core equals a weak pull, which equals a weak muscle-up. If your muscle-up is a muscle-up looks like you're doing the worm in the air, that full-body arch, it's a compensation, usually from a weak core. This is why the hollow body hold is one of those boring basics that you just can't be skipping in calisthenics. It strengthens your anterior core so you can resist spinal extension and keep your body hollow during the muscle-up instead of breaking down at the midline. One of the hidden blessings of calisthenics is that movements like muscle-ups, they expose your weak links fast. You need both the awareness to train your core and the discipline to actually do your homework. Hollow body holds are the preferred exercise here because they train the exact isometric core strength that muscle-ups demand. This is far more specific and beneficial than sit-ups or crunches, so skip those for now. Once your isometric core strength levels up, now your spine is going to be more stable. Your body, it's going to move as a connected unit and the whole movement is going to feel stronger and look cleaner. P.S. For those of you legends that are still here, here's a bonus hollow body progression that is perfect for muscle-ups. It strengthens your abs to withstand the dynamic demands of calisthenics, leading to less banana back and a bulletproof core. Now fellas, muscle-ups are easy to learn with progression, patience and persistence. Time is your best friend. Keep working at it and before you know it, you'll be bouncing over the bar like a kangaroo. Here's another Fitness FAQs video you simply must watch. More workout wisdom awaits you right here.

=== FILE: Why You Still Can't Hold Front Lever (Not Core Strength) [x8Q2TFkCZJ4].txt ===

terminal no amount of front lever technique is going to save you. Unless we've got our basic calisthenics up to scratch, anything that I teach you later on about front levers won't actually help unless you do this first. Horizontal pulling with inverted rows is the most overlooked movement. Everyone just spams pull-ups and they forget about rows, which is a big mistake. For the goal of front levers though, having a really good base with horizontal pulling is one of the best ways to fast track your progress. Interestingly, if we look at the front lever and look at an inverted row, these two exercises are actually more similar. They're both horizontal pulls and the joint angles of the upper body with the back working are more related compared to pull-ups. Also, the inverted row is perfect for strengthening up your mid-back muscles. These are the ones that are responsible for retraction of the shoulder blades. This is a key action that you'll need your body to be good at for the purposes of doing front levers. Without this level of inverted row strength, it's going to show in your lack of work capacity when it comes to front lever holds and training. It's going to help you so much having this mid-back strength and scapular endurance into retraction and depression. Inverted rows are often mistaken as a beginner exercise when, in fact, they can be overloaded with extra weight. This keeps the exercise difficult forever and you can continue challenging your mid-back and your scapula. It can build up an even greater surplus of strength. Now, doing inverted rows themselves won't automatically make you unlock this skill, but it's a foundation and that your body gets built on so that when you do go into specific lever exercises, the learning curve is going to be so much quicker than if you're skipping the basics completely. My favorite calisthenics exercise that translates to front levers is called the L-row. I'd consider this a great substitute for weighted inverted rows as a variation with the greatest carryover to front lever gains. This one builds up bent arm strength in your back and scaps in the horizontal plane of motion. This is a progression because now you're rowing the full weight of your body without your feet on the bench. You're essentially doing an advanced tuck with the legs extended. It's incredibly humbling how hard these are to do with that full range of motion. Elbows straight at the bottom and trying to pull until your elbows meet the sides. Form wise, make sure that you're keeping the body horizontal during this exercise because it's really tempting when you get tired to try and crunch the body. The challenge of bodyweight training is keeping yourself accountable. When it comes to technique, just stop your set if your form starts turning to trash. Or if you can't keep your technique on point, go back to inverted rows and build up your strength first. Now to ensure your back has well-rounded strength for the front lever, just get your weighted pull-up numbers up. I've coached many people over the years who can do pull-ups with two plates or more who automatically hold a front lever the first time they try it without any direct training. That's what's interesting about the front lever. If you have general back strength, it can be a shortcut to unlocking the skill. The same can't be said for planche. It's rare to see someone doing dips with a few plates automatically full planche without training it. Not sure why that's the case for pulling movements compared to pushing. Food for thought, basically. The heavier that you can pull for sets of five, the stronger you'll become and the easier your front lever journey will be. It's all about building up your absolute strength with lifting more added weight on your pull-ups. This way, when you go to do front levers where it's just handling your own bodyweight, there's a greater degree of mastery that's present. I'd recommend training your weighted pull-ups with a pronated grip shoulder width apart. Basically using the same setup that you would in a front lever for the greatest transfer. Now that you understand the importance of basics and you're not going to skip them, I hope, let's focus on the front lever. Problem two, skipping progressions. Skipping progressions is one of the biggest reasons that people stall or get injured in calisnacks. I'm talking doing full front lever attempts that you can't even hold. Being impatient, wanting to unlock everything right now. People just can't delay gratification and work on regressions and it's something that I wish you do. You see, front levers are all about leverage. Everyone should start in a tuck and as you get stronger, gradually extend the body all the way towards that full front lever. The most common mistake is A, not using the correct progression for your level and B, making big jumps between progressions. People rush to do the full front lever because they want to show off on social media. But here's the reality. Regular training is much more slow. It's about using a regression that you can actually do and one that's going to build your body. You wouldn't go in the gym and lift your 1RM on an exercise every time you go in. I hope at least. Don't treat calisthenics with this same mentality either. You've got to use your workouts to train, not test. The smartest approach is choosing a front lever progression that you can hold for around 10 to 20 second sets. Doing your front levers for this long is the equivalent of doing 5 to 10 reps on a full range of motion movement. This is a great heuristic that you can use when you're confused about how long to hold an exercise. Just divide the isometric number by 2 and you've got a rough intensity to work with. I wouldn't recommend doing holds of less than 5 seconds for regular training. This intensity is so high that it's going to be difficult to use the correct activation. Besides, if you just stick with the 10 to 20 second hold range, you're able to accumulate more volume, you've got more time under effort and this leads to more rapid learning and faster front lever gains. Bands. You've got to use bands for front levers because it gives you a huge advantage. If you're not making use of this tool in calisthenics, it's a big mistake. A common problem that people have is they can do an advanced tuck front lever for 20 seconds, but a straddle front lever fails after say 3 seconds. Bands, they're your best friend for bridging the gap between progressions. It allows you to do more on the advanced position at that longer lever while keeping the intensity possible to do those productive holds of at least 10 seconds. You don't need to train the hardest front lever progression that you can hold every single time. That's a big misconception. That mindset usually comes from insecurity. It's a fear that you're going to lose all of your gains because you're not pushing 100% every session. I've been able to maintain my full front lever for long periods, by just doing regressions like straddle front levers or even just advanced tuck halts. This shouldn't be a shock because you're still working the same movement pattern just under more manageable load and easier conditions. In many cases, activation in the movement is usually better because it's controlled rather than being forced at a max intensity. What matters most at the end of the day? Consistency. Some days you're going to feel weaker and that's normal. So give yourself permission to use easier front lever positions or train with bands when you need them. Taking a step back with intensity within a workout or even for a few weeks often leads to better long-term progress, less burnout and more enjoyment in the process. Problem. Poor scapular depression activation. For many people, the scapular is the missing link that's preventing them from holding a clean front lever. You can have decent back strength and follow the right progressions, but if you can't actively set and maintain scapular retraction and depression, you'll never reach your full potential. In calisthenics skills, failure isn't always due to a lack of strength. So how do we address it? Use activations. These are low fatigue drills that switch on the exact muscles and positions that a skill requires. It uses low to moderate intensity to wake up your nervous system and muscles. It targets specific joint actions, in this case straight arms and scapular movement. An activation improves your motor control and awareness of where your body is in space so you can feel the position before doing it in your training. Most importantly, activations reduce force leakage during the main skill. This is where you're losing out on strength when you're trying to express it in the position. When you combine proper scapular accessory work with your body weight basics and isometric holds, front lever mastery becomes a breeze. The scapular pull, it's your bread and butter activation exercise. This is all about depressing and retracting the shoulders with straight arms. You're trying to elevate your shoulders in the stretch and then contract them down into depression like a pullover. It's not about feeling the burn or building muscle. This is all about control. If you can smoothly move through this small but important range without shaking, it's teaching your body how to access the lats and shoulder stability that we need for the front lever. The horizontal scapular pull is a personal favorite. The same scapular action but now we're in a horizontal position which carries over better to the front lever. Just focus on clean retraction and depression. No bending the arms, not even a little bit. One or two short sets here is more than enough to prime your mid-back before front lever training and you'll really feel the difference. Learning the front lever isn't about shortcuts. It's a strength skill that's earned through getting damn good at your body weight basics, progressions and working on your weak links to unlock your full potential. Alright fellas, I want you to get even stronger at calisthenics. Watch this next video. I'm just here to help you. No drama, just straight up FAQs, education, wisdom and trying to give you the best gains possible. That's it man, just some wholesome content. No rage bait here, just fun facts.
